title: Maize Milk
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Young maize pounded, the juice squeezed out and boiled — a milk made from a cereal, and the only thing like it in the Ugandan record.
longDesc: Maize milk is young maize pounded in a mortar, the juice squeezed out and then boiled. It is a Lugbara preparation and it is genuinely unusual: nothing else in the Ugandan repertoire extracts a liquid from a cereal this way and drinks it. The maize has to be young — the milky stage, before the kernels harden — which is a narrow window in the growing season. The boiling is what makes it keep and what thickens it slightly.
ingredients: Young maize, at the milky stage
steps: Squeeze the juice out through a cloth or sieve.
chefTips: Young maize only, at the milky stage. Press a kernel and it should burst with a white liquid — that is the window, and it is short.
Pound rather than blend if you can. A blender shreds the husk material into the liquid and you cannot strain it all back out.
Squeeze it properly through cloth. What is left in the pulp is the drink.
Boil it. Raw cereal juice does not keep and the boiling also thickens it a little.

This belongs to a set of Lugbara drinks worth knowing: ebe'de or ibe'de is unsweetened tea, named after the scooping action because it is self-service; kuruku chai is lemongrass boiled in tea; anya i'di is millet porridge with groundnut or sesame paste; mengu i'di is cooked mango with the juice squeezed while cooling and mixed with sugar.
No quantities are documented for this in any source. Nothing here is estimated.
Like nearly all fresh-maize dishes, this exists because of a glut — it is what you do when the garden gives you more young maize than you can eat off the cob.
commonMistakes: Using mature maize, which gives almost no juice.
Not squeezing the pulp out properly.
Expecting it to keep like dairy milk.
sources: Adapted from the Wikipedia article on Lugbara cuisine, which records maize milk as young maize pounded with the juice squeezed and boiled. That is the entirety of the documented method and no quantities are given.

The related Lugbara drinks named in the same article are carried in the tips: ebe'de or ibe'de, unsweetened tea named after the scooping action and taken self-service; kuruku chai, lemongrass boiled in tea; anya i'di, millet porridge with groundnut or sesame paste; and mengu i'di, cooked mango with the juice squeezed while cooling and mixed with sugar.
That article carries only three references, including web archives and blog material on Lugbara culture, so its detail is treated as a lead rather than as established fact.
healthBenefits: Young maize supplies fibre, folate, thiamine and the carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin.
Dairy-free and naturally free of gluten.
Uses maize at its most nutritious stage, before the starch sets.
culturalNote: Squeezing a drink out of young maize is the sort of thing that happens where a crop arrives all at once and has to be used. It also puts the Lugbara kitchen alongside the maize-milk traditions of the Americas without any contact between them — the same plant suggesting the same idea twice.
